---
title: "The Doubling Cube"
subtitle: "Janowski's model has three equity formulas. Measured against rollouts, two are right and one is not."
toc-depth: 2
jupyter: python3
---

Rick Janowski's cube-life-index model is how a cubeless evaluation becomes a cube
decision. GNU Backgammon and eXtreme Gammon both ship it, and its published
constant — $x = 0.68$ for contact positions — has stood essentially unchanged
since 1993. It has rarely been *measured*, because doing so needs observed
cubeful equities for a large and varied set of real positions.

Those observations turned out to be sitting in a file this project already had
on disk. The BGSage money benchmark rolled 42,636 candidate positions out to
completion with the cube live, recording for each one a **measured cubeful
equity** next to the cubeless probabilities for the same position — and the cube
sits in a different place across them, which is what makes the model separable.

**This page is about the model, not about our engine.** Raccoon is the
instrument, not the subject. A better map from cubeless probabilities to cubeful
equity is worth having on its own terms, most of all to anyone evaluating cube
decisions without a deep search behind them. Stronger play follows from it; it is
not what is being optimised here.

The short answer: **the three formulas fail in three different ways, and the
worst failure sits exactly where cube decisions get made.** When your opponent
owns the cube, the model is correct everywhere. When *you* own it, the model is
correct across the 93% of positions far from a cashing decision — and then
undershoots by up to 0.09 in the narrow band just below the cash point. When the
cube is **centred** it is wrong throughout — too optimistic when you are behind,
too pessimistic when you are ahead, crossing over near even money. A residual
that changes sign cannot be removed by any constant.

Those are smaller numbers than an earlier version of this page reported, and the
difference is instructive enough to state up front. Janowski's formulas give the
**no-double** equity — what a position is worth if the cube stays where it is —
while a rollout reference always includes the option to double. Comparing them
directly charges the formula for an option it was never asked to price, and doing
so inflated the centred error from 0.043 to 0.064 and produced two mechanisms
that turned out to be largely artefacts. [Four positions checked in GNU
Backgammon](#check-it-yourself) settled it: GNUBG's own *No double* line
reproduces these formulas closely, and its *optimal* line matches the rollout.

Everything here is cubeless-money play with the Jacoby rule and beavers on,
matching the benchmark. Match play, where the score changes every take point, is
out of scope.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import json
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
plt.rcParams["figure.dpi"] = 120

# Cube location is an identity encoding, so the three hues are categorical and
# assigned in a fixed order. Marker shape repeats the same distinction, so the
# panels stay readable without colour.
C_OWN, C_CEN, C_OPP = "#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a"
LOC = {"player":   (C_OWN, "o", "we own the cube"),
       "centered": (C_CEN, "s", "cube centred"),
       "opponent": (C_OPP, "^", "opponent owns it")}

R = Path("../experiments/exp024-cube/results")

def load(name):
    return json.loads((R / f"{name}.json").read_text())

def variant(source, name):
    stem = f"{source} :: {name}".lower()
    for ch in " ()/-.,":
        stem = stem.replace(ch, "_")
    return load(stem.strip("_"))

FIT = load("cube_equity_fit")
SCAT = load("cube_equity_scatter")
DIAG = load("residual_diagnostics")
FLOOR = load("cube_blind_floor")
BASE = variant("reference", "baseline")
```

## The model is three formulas

A network evaluates a position *cubelessly*: six probabilities for winning or
losing a plain game, a gammon, or a backgammon, if the game were played out with
no cube. Under real rules that game never happens. Janowski's model says what
those probabilities are worth once the cube is on the table.

It starts by compressing the outcome distribution into two numbers — the average
value of a win and of a loss:

$$W=\frac{\sum_i i \cdot P(\text{win } i)}{P(\text{win})}
\qquad
L=\frac{\sum_i i \cdot P(\text{lose } i)}{P(\text{lose})}$$

A gammonless position has $W = L = 1$. Two extremes can then be solved exactly. A
**dead cube** can never be turned again, so the game plays out at the current
stake and a take risks $2L-1$ to gain $2W+1$ — the familiar 25% take point. A
**live cube** is redoubled at exactly the right moment every time, which adds a
constant bonus and gives the continuous model's 20%. Real positions sit between,
at a fraction $x$ — the **cube life index**, 0 for dead, 1 for live.

What matters for everything below is that the model then produces **three
different equity formulas, one per cube location** (Janowski's equations 5–7):

$$E_O = C_V\left[p(W + L + 0.5x) - L\right] \qquad \text{we own the cube}$$

$$E_U = C_V\left[p(W + L + 0.5x) - L - 0.5x\right] \qquad \text{opponent owns it}$$

$$E_C = \frac{4C_V}{4-x}\left[p(W + L + 0.5x) - L - 0.25x\right] \qquad \text{centred}$$

Every take point, cash point and doubling point in the paper is derived by
setting two of these equal. So the model stands or falls on them, and — crucially
— **they can fail independently**. That is what makes the measurement below
possible, and it is not something a cube decision can reveal: a double compares
only two locations at a time.

One property of $x$ matters later. It is meant to be a **physical property of the
position** — its volatility. Janowski derives it as "proportional to the degree
of cube-life of the position and inversely proportional to its long-term
volatility". The same position has the same volatility whoever is holding the
cube, so $x$ cannot legitimately depend on cube location.

## What GNU Backgammon and XG actually implement

Two details, both easy to get wrong when reproducing these engines.

**They use a piecewise-linear centred formula, not the one above.** GNUBG pins
the live-cube equity at the points where it is known — $-1$ at the take point,
$+1$ at the cash point, $-L$ and $+W$ at the extremes — and interpolates linearly
between them, with the outer segments clamped to $\pm 1$ under Jacoby. That is a
*substitution* for equation (7), not an approximation of it, and it is what
`raccoon/cube/janowski.py` implements because it is what we are measuring against.

**The closed form is a leaf evaluator, not the cube engine.** GNUBG does not
convert a static evaluation into a cube decision and stop. It runs a cubeful
search, making cube decisions at each node and applying Janowski only at the
leaves. The formula is to the cube engine what the value head is to our checker
play: the thing at the bottom of a tree.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Janowski's three formulas in a gammonless position (W = L = 1) at the published index x = 0.68 — pure theory, no data. Read the y-axis carefully: these curves are the equity of NOT turning the cube, which is what the formulas are defined to give. Above the cash point that is the wrong quantity to act on — you double, your opponent passes, and gammonless the position is worth exactly +1 (dash-dotted). The gap between the blue curve and that ceiling is not an error in the formula; it is the difference between holding the cube and using it."
from raccoon.cube import janowski as J

p = np.linspace(0.001, 0.999, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.4))
cp = J.cash_point(1.0, 1.0, 0.68)
for owner in ("player", "centered", "opponent"):
    colour, marker, label = LOC[owner]
    y = [J.cl2cf_money((pi, 0, 0, 0, 0), owner, 0.68, jacoby=False) for pi in p]
    ax.plot(p, y, color=colour, label=label, lw=2)
# What the position is actually worth if you take the cube action: above the cash
# point you double, your opponent passes, and gammonless that is exactly +1.
own = [J.cl2cf_money((pi, 0, 0, 0, 0), "player", 0.68, jacoby=False) for pi in p]
ax.plot(p, np.minimum(np.maximum(own, np.where(p >= cp, 1.0, -np.inf)), 1.0),
        color="#111111", ls="-.", lw=1.4, label="value if you cash (owned)")
ax.plot(p, 2 * p - 1, "--", color="#666666", lw=1, label="dead cube (x = 0)")
ax.axvline(cp, color="#555555", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.text(cp - 0.015, -0.92, "cash point", fontsize=8, color="#555555", ha="right")
ax.axhline(0, color="#999999", lw=0.6)
ax.set_xlabel("cubeless winning probability")
ax.set_ylabel("equity if the cube is NOT turned")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="upper left")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

> What is Janowski's model? → **Three equity formulas sharing one parameter**,
> one per cube location, from which every take point and doubling point is
> derived. They can be wrong independently, and $x$ is meant to describe the
> position, not the cube's location.

## How to measure it

Cube models are usually argued about rather than measured, because the references
are expensive. The BGSage money benchmark has them, but not all of its numbers
are equal and the distinction turned out to matter more than anything else here.

### Only some references are measurements

Every entry carries an `eval_level` recording how it was produced.

* **`Rollout`** — 1,296 trials **played to completion** with the cube live and
  variance reduction on. The equity is an observed average of real games, with a
  standard error around ±0.005 at 95%.
* **`3-ply`** — a cubeful search which calls Janowski at *its own leaves*
  (`cube.cpp:670`).

Scoring a Janowski variant against the second kind is close to scoring it against
itself, and the data says so plainly. On the benchmark's cube decisions, the
published model measures PR **0.649** against search-derived references and
**5.406** against rolled-out ones — and re-fitting the index is worth +0.117 ±
0.210 (nothing) on the first and +3.049 ± 0.641 on the second. Only the measured
references are used below.

### The checker rollouts are the better instrument

The benchmark's *cube* decisions are the obvious place to look, and they are not
the best one. Only 700 of them have rolled-out references. Its **checker**
decisions have 42,636 rolled-out candidates, each carrying a measured cubeful
equity beside the cubeless probabilities for the same position, with the parent
decision recording where the cube sat. That is 60 times the data, it observes the
equity map directly rather than a decision downstream of it, and — decisively —
the cube location varies across it, so each of the three formulas can be tested
**on its own**.

### What these references still are not

* The **payoff is empirical, the policy is not.** Games are played out and points
  counted, but the cube decisions made *during* each rollout come from a bot that
  also uses Janowski. So these measure equity under Janowski-quality cube play,
  not optimal cube play. Policy error can only lower realised equity and its cost
  is second-order near a decision threshold, so this understates what a better
  model could reach rather than overstating it.
* They are **post-move** positions, so the opponent is on roll, whereas cube
  decisions are pre-roll. Janowski's formulas do not model whose turn it is — the
  probabilities are supposed to carry that — so one index across both is itself
  an approximation. There is a hint below that this matters.
* **No position is observed at more than one cube location.** A rollout values
  the position as it actually stood. $E_O$ and $E_C$ are never measured together,
  which is why an inconsistency between them cannot be caught by the data at all.

> Can Janowski be measured with what we have? → **Yes — 42,636 observed cubeful
> equities**, spanning all three cube locations, at zero play cost. But only the
> rolled-out third of the benchmark can judge it; against search-derived
> references the model scores eight times better than it deserves.

## Which formula is broken

Each formula, fitted independently against the measured equities for the
positions where that cube location actually applied:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print("| formula | cube location | positions | bias @ 0.68 | RMSE @ 0.68 | "
      "best-fit x | RMSE there |")
print("|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|")
for owner in ("player", "centered", "opponent"):
    v = FIT["by_cube_location"][owner]
    print(f"| $E_{v['formula'][-1]}$ | {v['label']} | {v['n']:,} | "
          f"{v['bias_at_published_x']:+.4f} | {v['rmse_at_published_x']:.4f} | "
          f"{v['best_x']:.3f} | {v['rmse_at_best_x']:.4f} |")
pl = FIT["pooled"]
print(f"\nOne index applied everywhere — what the engines ship — gives RMSE "
      f"**{pl['rmse_at_published_x']:.4f}** at 0.68, improving to "
      f"{pl['rmse_at_best_x']:.4f} at {pl['best_x']:.3f}. Almost all of that "
      f"error is one formula.")
```

$E_O$ is essentially exact at the published constant: a bias of +0.0001 across
17,210 positions, and re-fitting the index moves the RMSE by 3%. $E_U$ is nearly
as good. Both want $x \approx 0.72$ — close to each other and to 0.68, which is
what a genuine property of the position should look like.

$E_C$ is a different object. Biased twenty-five times more, three and a half
times noisier, and to reach its best it demands $x = 0.94$: a cube one
twentieth away from perfectly live, in ordinary contact positions where the other
two formulas say 0.72. Even there it lands at 0.0295 — still **60% worse** than
the other two achieve for free at the published constant.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Modelled against observed cubeful equity at the published x = 0.68, for a 12,000-position sample of the rolled-out candidates. The diagonal is perfect prediction. This is the orienting view: it shows the model is broadly calibrated across the whole equity range and how the positions are distributed, but it cannot resolve the differences this page is about — cubeful equity spans roughly ±1.6, so an error of 0.05 is under 2% of the axis. The next figure puts that error on its own scale."
owner_idx = np.array(SCAT["owner_idx"])
obs = np.array(SCAT["observed"])
mod = np.array(SCAT["modelled_published"])
resid = mod - obs
owners = SCAT["owners"]
lim = (-1.6, 1.6)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7.6, 2.9), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, owner in zip(axes, ("player", "centered", "opponent")):
    colour, marker, label = LOC[owner]
    m = owner_idx == owners.index(owner)
    ax.plot(lim, lim, color="#555555", lw=1, zorder=3)
    ax.scatter(obs[m], mod[m], s=3, alpha=0.18, color=colour, marker=marker,
               linewidths=0, zorder=2)
    ax.set_title(label, fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_xlim(*lim); ax.set_ylim(*lim)
    ax.set_xlabel("observed (rollout)", fontsize=8)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
axes[0].set_ylabel("modelled (Janowski)", fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Broadly calibrated, and not much else can be read off it. Putting the *error* on
the y-axis instead resolves what the diagonal hides:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The same data and the same x-axis as the plot above, with the error moved to the y-axis. That is the whole change: a 0.05 miss is invisible against a ±1.6 equity range and obvious against a ±0.22 one. Note that the centred panel occupies a narrower slice of the x-axis than the other two — with a centred cube somebody doubles, so realised equity rarely strays far past ±1, whereas an owned cube can run to ±2 and beyond. E_O and E_U sit in a tight band; E_C is three times wider and visibly tilted, running high on the left and low on the right."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7.6, 2.9), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, owner in zip(axes, ("player", "centered", "opponent")):
    colour, marker, label = LOC[owner]
    m = owner_idx == owners.index(owner)
    ax.axhline(0, color="#333333", lw=1, zorder=3)
    ax.scatter(obs[m], resid[m], s=3, alpha=0.16, color=colour, marker=marker,
               linewidths=0, zorder=2)
    v = FIT["by_cube_location"][owner]
    ax.set_title(f"{label}\nRMSE {v['rmse_at_published_x']:.4f}", fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.22, 0.22)
    ax.set_xlim(*lim)
    ax.set_xlabel("observed (rollout)", fontsize=8)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
axes[0].set_ylabel("model − observed", fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The picture matches the table. Two panels are a narrow band about zero; the
centred one is three times wider and tilted, high on the left and low on the
right — the sign change that later sections take apart.

Worth stating plainly, because it is an easy way to fool yourself: the diagonal
plot above is *not* evidence of a good model. All three panels would look like a
clean diagonal even if the errors were several times larger, because cubeful
equity spans ±1.6 and the differences at stake are a few hundredths. Any check of
this kind has to end on an axis scaled to the error, not to the quantity.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The same errors split by BGSage's game-plan classification. The centred series is the widest in every panel, so this is not a quirk of one position type, and the same tilt appears in each: too optimistic where the position is losing, too pessimistic where it is winning. Per-plan RMSE is in the panel titles; the table below gives it numerically."
GP_RMSE = FIT["by_game_plan"]
plan_idx = np.array(SCAT["plan_idx"])
plans = SCAT["plans"]
order = [p for p in ("purerace", "racing", "attacking", "priming", "anchoring")
         if p in plans]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(7.6, 5.2), sharex=True, sharey=True)
# Materialise before zipping: zip pulls the 6th axis and discards it when the
# plan list runs out, which would leave nothing for the legend panel.
flat = list(axes.flat)
for ax, plan in zip(flat, order):
    pm = plan_idx == plans.index(plan)
    ax.axhline(0, color="#333333", lw=1, zorder=3)
    for owner in ("player", "opponent", "centered"):
        colour, marker, _ = LOC[owner]
        m = pm & (owner_idx == owners.index(owner))
        ax.scatter(obs[m], resid[m], s=6, alpha=0.30, color=colour,
                   marker=marker, linewidths=0, zorder=2)
    rm = GP_RMSE[plan]["centered"]["rmse_at_published_x"]
    ax.set_title(f"{plan}  (n = {int(pm.sum()):,})\ncentred RMSE {rm:.4f}",
                 fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_xlim(*lim); ax.set_ylim(-0.22, 0.22)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)
# Bottom-row panels label the x-axis; so does any top-row panel with an empty
# slot beneath it, which sharex would otherwise leave without tick labels.
ncols = axes.shape[1]
for i, ax in enumerate(flat):
    if i >= len(order):
        continue
    if i + ncols >= len(order):
        ax.set_xlabel("observed (rollout)", fontsize=8.5)
        ax.tick_params(labelbottom=True, labelsize=8)
for ax in axes[:, 0]:
    ax.set_ylabel("model − observed", fontsize=8.5)

# The sixth panel is free, so the legend goes there instead of crowding the plots.
spare = flat[-1] if len(order) < len(flat) else None
if spare is not None:
    spare.axis("off")
    handles = [plt.Line2D([], [], color=LOC[o][0], marker=LOC[o][1], ls="",
                          ms=9, label=LOC[o][2])
               for o in ("player", "centered", "opponent")]
    spare.legend(handles=handles, frameon=False, fontsize=9.5, loc="center",
                 title="cube position", title_fontsize=9.5)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

RMSE at the published index, by game plan and cube location:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

order = [p for p in ("purerace", "racing", "attacking", "priming", "anchoring")
```

Two independent checks say the method is sound rather than the model being
uniformly bad. Let the index float freely against the take/pass line alone, told
nothing about what it should be:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
dv = DIAG["dt_validation"]
print(f"Fitted across all {dv['all']['n']:,} rolled-out cube positions, the "
      f"take/pass index comes out at **{dv['all']['best_x_by_rmse']:.3f}** — "
      f"against GNU Backgammon's published 0.68. Within pure races it comes out "
      f"at {dv['by_game_plan']['purerace']['best_x_by_rmse']:.3f}, against "
      f"GNUBG's documented 0.60 race constant.")
```

The measurement reproduces both published constants without being told either.

> Which formula is broken? → **The centred one**, at RMSE 0.043 against 0.019 and
> 0.016 for the other two, needing $x = 0.92$ to reach an accuracy the others
> beat for free at the published constant. But averages hide *where* the failures
> are, which the next section takes apart.

## Where in the range each formula fails

The averages above hide something the curves hint at. Plot the error against
distance from the model's own **cash point** — the winning chance above which
your opponent should pass a double, so the position is simply worth $+1$:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The same errors as the scatters above, on the same axis, distilled to bin means with 95% intervals. Zero is agreement; below zero the model says the position is worth less than it proved to be. The intervals are clustered on the checker decision, because candidates within one decision are the same position played different ways and are anything but independent — clustering roughly doubles them, and treating candidates as independent would have made every bin look about twice as certain as it is. Marker area is proportional to the number of positions in the bin, so the thin tails do not read as loudly as the dense middle. E_O tracks zero until about 55% and then sags through the run-up to a cashing decision, recovering once the cash is banked. E_C is off in both directions — too optimistic when behind, too pessimistic when ahead — crossing zero near even money, a change of sign no single constant can absorb. E_U sits on zero from about a third upward; its two leftmost points drift high but rest on under 150 positions each, since being behind while your opponent owns the cube is a rare place to be."
PROF = FIT["equity_profile"]                    # winning-chance bins, used in prose
EPROF = FIT["equity_profile_by_observed"]       # equity bins, plotted here
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.6))
for owner in ("player", "centered", "opponent"):
    colour, marker, label = LOC[owner]
    bins = [b for b in EPROF[owner]["bins"] if b["n"] >= 60]
    xs = [b["eq_mean"] for b in bins]
    ys = [b["modelled"] - b["observed"] for b in bins]
    errs = [b["ci95_clustered"] for b in bins]
    sizes = [12 + 90 * (b["n"] / 2500) ** 0.5 for b in bins]
    ax.plot(xs, ys, color=colour, lw=1.4, alpha=0.7, zorder=2)
    ax.errorbar(xs, ys, yerr=errs, fmt="none", ecolor=colour, elinewidth=1.2,
                capsize=2.5, alpha=0.9, zorder=2)
    ax.scatter(xs, ys, s=sizes, color=colour, marker=marker, label=label,
               zorder=3, edgecolors="white", linewidths=0.6)
ax.axhline(0, color="#333333", lw=1.2, zorder=1)
ax.set_xlabel("observed equity (rollout)")
ax.set_ylabel("model − observed (points)")
ax.set_xlim(*lim)
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8.5, loc="lower left")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print("| observed equity | $E_O$ we own | $E_C$ centred | $E_U$ opponent owns |")
print("|---|---:|---:|---:|")
edges = sorted({(b["eq_lo"], b["eq_hi"]) for o in EPROF for b in EPROF[o]["bins"]})
for lo, hi in edges:
    cells = []
    for owner in ("player", "centered", "opponent"):
        b = next((b for b in EPROF[owner]["bins"]
                  if b["eq_lo"] == lo and b["n"] >= 60), None)
        cells.append("—" if b is None else
                     f"{b['modelled'] - b['observed']:+.3f} <small>(n={b['n']:,})</small>")
    if all(c == "—" for c in cells):
        continue
    print(f"| {lo:+.1f} to {hi:+.1f} | " + " | ".join(cells) + " |")
```

Three readings.

**$E_U$ is correct wherever it has weight.** From about $-0.2$ equity upward it
sits on zero — within 0.003 across more than 8,000 positions. Its two leftmost
points drift positive but rest on around a hundred positions each: being the
underdog while your opponent holds the cube is a rare place to be.

**$E_O$ is correct until the position is nearly won.** Across everything below
zero equity it tracks the rollouts within 0.009, on 13,000 positions. Then it
sags — $-0.041$ by $+0.5$, $-0.080$ by $+0.9$ — and snaps back to zero above
$+1.0$. That band is thin, a few hundred positions out of 17,210, which is why
the aggregate RMSE of 0.0186 barely notices it. It is also exactly the range in
which a cashing decision is live.

**$E_C$ is wrong in both directions.** About $+0.043$ when the position is worth
half a point *against* you, crossing zero near even equity, and $-0.099$ when it
is worth two-thirds of a point *for* you. A residual that changes sign cannot be
removed by any constant, any index, or any offset, which is what separates a
mis-specified formula from a mis-set parameter.

**None of this is chance.** The intervals above are clustered on the checker
decision, which roughly doubles them against the naive version, and even so every
$E_C$ bin sits many interval-widths from zero — $+0.043 \pm 0.002$ on the left,
$-0.099 \pm 0.007$ on the right. Exactly two bins in the whole figure are
consistent with zero, and both are bins where the claim is that the model is
*right*: $E_O$ at even equity ($-0.002 \pm 0.004$) and $E_O$ above $+1.0$
($-0.004 \pm 0.008$), the latter confirming that its recovery past the cashing
range is real rather than a thin-data artefact.

The $E_O$ sag has a mechanism worth naming, because it is the one thing here that
is clearly a *modelling* choice rather than a measurement question. The model
blends a dead-cube branch with a live-cube branch in fixed proportion,
$(1-x)E_{\text{dead}} + xE_{\text{live}}$. As a position approaches its cash
point the live branch has reached its ceiling of $+1$ while the dead branch is
still only $2p-1 \approx 0.6$, so the blend drags the answer down by roughly
$(1-x) \times 0.4$. That is why the sag appears where it does on the axis above:
equity around $+0.5$ to $+1.0$ is where a position is close to cashable. But a
position near its cash point does not *need* future cube efficiency — you double
and your opponent passes. A fixed weight is defensible in the middle of the range
and not near the boundary.

### Is the owned-cube sag about cashing, or about playing on for a gammon?

Both would show up as the model undervaluing a nearly-won position, and they call
for different fixes. They make opposite predictions, so the data separates them.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
BD = FIT["branch_divergence"]["bins"]
print("| observed equity | positions | observed | blend at 0.68 | live branch (x=1) | "
      "dead branch | branch gap | gammon-win rate |")
print("|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|")
for b in BD:
    print(f"| {b['eq_lo']:+.1f} to {b['eq_hi']:+.1f} | {b['n']:,} | "
          f"{b['observed']:.3f} | {b['blend_x068']:.3f} | {b['live_x1']:.3f} | "
          f"{b['dead']:.3f} | {b['branch_divergence']:.3f} | "
          f"{b['gammon_win_rate']:.3f} |")
```

**It is the cash.** In the sag band the *live* branch is nearly right — 0.921
against an observed 0.890 — while the blend gives 0.809. The live branch is the
one that assumes the cube gets used efficiently, so what the model is missing is
the cube's value, not gammon equity.

The gammon rates confirm it from the other side. Through the sag the gammon-win
rate is **0.052**: these positions have almost no gammon to play on for, so
cashing is the plan. Just above, where the model has no measurable error at all,
the rate is **0.208** and every position is past the cash point — there the
player *is* playing on for a gammon, and the model handles it correctly, because
the live branch's segment above the cash point runs from $+1$ up to $+W$ and
captures exactly that.

The sharper statement is arithmetic. The blend can only do damage where the two
branches disagree, and the measured error tracks that disagreement almost
proportionally: the branch gap peaks at 0.348 exactly where the error peaks at
0.081, and collapses to 0.123 where the error vanishes. A fixed 32% weight on the
dead branch is a fixed *fraction* of a gap that is not fixed at all.

Note that most of the sag band is not even past the cash point — 1% at
$+0.6$ to $+0.8$, 31% at $+0.8$ to $+1.0$. So this is not "the model fails to
notice you can cash right now". It is that a player who owns the cube, is
winning, and has no gammon to chase will convert that cube efficiently, and the
published index of 0.68 prices that too cheaply. The effective index in this band
is nearer 0.9.

## Is it the Jacoby rule? Unresolved — and this page has been wrong about it twice

Everything below assumes the benchmark's reference equities were generated with
the Jacoby rule in force. They were, and it is worth showing rather than
asserting, because if it were false every centred number on this page would be
measuring the wrong model. The generator passes `jacoby=True` at each of its
analyzer call sites and leaves the default `jacoby=True` elsewhere, at `away1 =
away2 = 0` — money play — and the engine's `CubeInfo::jacoby_active()` is
`jacoby && is_money() && owner == CENTERED`, the same predicate as
[`janowski.jacoby_active`](https://github.com/lassehjorthmadsen/raccoon/blob/main/raccoon/cube/janowski.py).

The payoffs also say so on their own, which is the stronger check, since it does
not depend on the source tree matching the one that produced the file. Jacoby
suppresses gammons *only while the cube is centred*, so an owned cube is a
matched control: same rollout machinery, same units, and gammons paying double.
Equity here is in units of the current cube, so a gammon is worth 2.0 wherever
the cube stands.

The test is whether equity **rises with the gammon rate**. Among near-certain
wins, where the gammon is the only thing left to play for:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
JIF = FIT["jacoby_in_force"]
BY = JIF["by_cube_location"]
print(f"| gammon-win rate | centred: n | equity | cubeless | | opponent owns: n "
      f"| equity | cubeless |")
print("|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|")
cen = {(b["g_lo"], b["g_hi"]): b for b in BY["centered"]["gammon_slope"]}
opp = {(b["g_lo"], b["g_hi"]): b for b in BY["opponent"]["gammon_slope"]}
for k in sorted(set(cen) | set(opp)):
    c, o = cen.get(k), opp.get(k)
    f = lambda d, key: f"{d[key]:.3f}" if d else "—"
    print(f"| {k[0]:.1f}–{k[1]:.1f} | {c['n'] if c else 0:,} | "
          f"{f(c,'mean_equity')} | {f(c,'mean_cubeless_equity')} | | "
          f"{o['n'] if o else 0:,} | {f(o,'mean_equity')} | "
          f"{f(o,'mean_cubeless_equity')} |")
```

With the cube **owned**, measured equity tracks cubeless equity all the way up:
`{python} f"{opp[(0.0,0.1)]['mean_equity']:.3f}"` to
`{python} f"{opp[(0.4,1.0)]['mean_equity']:.3f}"` as the gammon rate climbs.
With the cube **centred**, it decouples and stays pinned near
`{python} f"{cen[(0.0,0.1)]['mean_equity']:.2f}"` while cubeless equity rises to
`{python} f"{cen[(0.4,1.0)]['mean_cubeless_equity']:.3f}"`. Gammons buy nothing
while the cube sits in the middle. That is the Jacoby rule, measured — and the
owned column is what rules out "those are simply different positions".

The same thing shows in the extremes. Only
`{python} str(BY['centered']['n_gammon_favourite'])` centred candidates are
odds-on to win a gammon at all — with Jacoby off, playing on for one would be
free and they would be common — and they top out at
`{python} f"{BY['centered']['max_equity_gammon_favourite']:.3f}"`. The owned-cube
control has `{python} f"{BY['opponent']['n_gammon_favourite']:,}"` of them,
averaging `{python} f"{BY['opponent']['mean_equity_gammon_favourite']:.3f}"`.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Then why does any centred position exceed +1?

Jacoby caps the *undoubled* payoff at one point, not the position. Doubling and
being taken pays 2, and once the cube moves Jacoby no longer applies. So values
above +1 exist; they are just rare, because cashing almost always dominates.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
A = JIF["centred_above_one"]
print(f"Exactly **{A['n']} of {BY['centered']['n']:,}** centred candidates are "
      f"worth more than +1. They average p(win) {A['mean_p_win']:.3f} with only "
      f"{A['mean_p_win_gammon']:.3f} gammon wins (highest "
      f"{A['max_p_win_gammon']:.3f}) and cubeless equity "
      f"{A['mean_cubeless_equity']:.3f}, for a measured "
      f"{A['mean_equity']:.3f} — peaking at {A['max_equity']:.3f}.")
```

They are not gammonish; they are strong and volatile, positions where the
opponent still has a take at the moment the cube goes over. Averaging a hair
above a point is what "usually cash, occasionally get taken" looks like. An
earlier version of this section argued from a ceiling at +1 instead of from the
gammon slope, which overstated the case: the ceiling is a tendency, the flat
slope is the actual signature.
:::

> Was the benchmark generated with Jacoby on? → **yes**, confirmed from the
> generator's source and independently from the payoffs: with the cube owned,
> equity rises with the gammon rate; with it centred, it does not.

The natural suspect for a centred-cube-only failure is the Jacoby rule, since it
is the one part of the model that applies only to a centred cube. It does two
things: it clamps the outer segments of the live-cube curve to $\pm 1$, and it
makes the dead-cube branch $2p - 1$ instead of the full cubeless equity, because
a cube that never turns never activates gammons.

The dead branch is the interesting one. It is a correct description of its own
branch, but it carries weight $1-x = 0.32$ in positions where the cube is
overwhelmingly likely to be turned — so a position facing heavy gammon *losses*
takes roughly a third of its value from a branch pretending those losses are
free. That predicts a residual scaling with gammon **asymmetry**, P(lose gammon)
minus P(win gammon).

It half-holds, and not in the shape the mechanism predicts:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
JD = FIT["jacoby_dead_branch"]
print(f"Across {JD['n']:,} centred positions the residual's correlation with "
      f"gammon asymmetry is **{JD['corr_gammon_asymmetry']:+.3f}** — but with "
      f"winning chance it is {JD['corr_winning_probability']:+.3f}, and the two "
      f"are entangled. Within narrow bands of winning chance:\n")
print("| winning chance | positions | correlation with gammon asymmetry |")
print("|---|---:|---:|")
for b in JD["within_p_band"]:
    print(f"| {b['p_lo']:.0%}–{b['p_hi']:.0%} | {b['n']:,} | "
          f"{b['corr_resid_asymmetry']:+.2f} |")
```

The sign **flips**: negative when behind, positive when ahead. A Jacoby
dead-branch artefact should push one way throughout. So whatever this is, it is
not cleanly the mechanism described above.

What does survive is cruder: simply not zeroing gammons in the dead branch fits
better, even though that is wrong for the branch's own definition.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print("| dead-cube branch | RMSE | bias in the worst gammon-asymmetry quartile |")
print("|---|---:|---:|")
a, b = JD["as_shipped"], JD["dead_branch_keeps_gammons"]
print(f"| as shipped, $2p-1$ | {a['rmse']:.4f} | {a['bias_worst_asymmetry_quartile']:+.4f} |")
print(f"| keeping gammons | {b['rmse']:.4f} | {b['bias_worst_asymmetry_quartile']:+.4f} |")
```

So the Jacoby handling is *implicated* — the numbers move when you change it —
but the mechanism is not established, and this page has now been wrong about it
in both directions. It is recorded as an open question rather than a finding.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## Two earlier versions of this section, and why both were wrong

**Version one** claimed Jacoby was ruled out, on three tests. It checked the
±1 clamp's *reach* rather than the dead branch — Jacoby has two effects and the
argument conflated them. It measured correlation against the **total** gammon
rate, which is near zero by construction because symmetric gammons cancel. And it
used 551 pre-roll cube positions rather than 14,612 rolled-out ones.

**Version two** corrected those and claimed Jacoby was confirmed, on a +0.563
correlation with gammon asymmetry that survived within bands of winning chance.
But that was measured against the **no-double** residual, which was itself
inflated by not applying the opponent's cube action. On the corrected residual
the within-band correlations change sign, and the finding does not hold.

Both errors share a shape: a mechanism was proposed, a statistic was found that
matched it, and the statistic was not stress-tested against the alternative that
something else produced it.
:::

## Check it yourself — and what the check returned

A large error in a formula two major engines have shipped for thirty years should
be independently verifiable, not taken on this page's arithmetic. So the
worst-fitting centred-cube positions were extracted with GNU Position IDs and
checked in GNU Backgammon's own money play. The check changed the paper's
conclusion.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
G = load("gnubg_spot_check")
print("| GNU Position ID | GNUBG *No double* | Janowski (no double) | "
      "GNUBG optimal | rollout | GNUBG's action |")
print("|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|")
for q in G["positions"]:
    opt = q["gnubg_nd"] if q["gnubg_action"].startswith("No double") else q["gnubg_dt"]
    print(f"| `{q['position_id']}` | {q['gnubg_nd']:+.3f} | {q['janowski_nd']:+.4f} | "
          f"{opt:+.3f} | {q['rollout']:+.4f} | {q['gnubg_action']} |")
```

All values from the on-roll player's side. Three things fall out, and the first
is the one that mattered.

**Janowski's no-double equity reproduces GNUBG's *No double* line.** On the
second position they agree to 0.001, on the third to 0.007. That validates this
implementation against a shipping engine — the arithmetic here is GNUBG's
arithmetic.

**The rollout is the *optimal-play* value, not the no-double value.** On the
first two positions GNUBG's proper action is Double/Take, worth +0.894 and
+0.959, and the rollouts are +0.9248 and +0.9743. An earlier version of this page
compared the no-double formula against those rollouts and reported a 0.23-point
error. Most of it was that mismatch. Correcting it — applying the cube action to
the player who actually holds it, which in a post-move position is the opponent —
cut the measured centred error from RMSE 0.064 to 0.043 and dissolved the large
positive bias when behind.

**A real closed-form miss survives, and search recovers it.** On the fourth
position Janowski gives −0.500 where GNUBG's 3-ply says −0.731 and the rollout
says −0.7429. Here the formula genuinely is off by nearly a quarter of a point,
GNUBG's search finds the right answer, and the closed form on its own does not.
That is the pattern this page argued for, now observed rather than inferred: the
formula is a leaf evaluator, and the engines' searches carry it.

The third position is the awkward one. Janowski and GNUBG's 3-ply agree at about
−0.845, while the rollout says −1.077. Both are a quarter-point optimistic
against 1,296 played-out games. GNUBG flags a beaver at 31.5% there and the
rollouts were run with beavers on, which may account for part of it; it is not
resolved here.

**Why this page could not run the check itself.** The `gnubg_nn` binding refuses
money play outright — `evaluate_cube_decision` raises "Not implemented for money"
— and `cubeful_rollout` returns undocumented fields. A long-match stand-in
produced incoherent numbers across plies and is not reported. The figures above
were read from the GUI by hand; their provenance is recorded in
`gnubg_spot_check.json` alongside the generated positions, so they are labelled
as an external observation rather than as something this repository computed.

## exp024, pre-registered

**Hypothesis.** Janowski's published cube-life index is mis-set: re-fitting $x$
recovers most of the cube-decision error that $x = 0.68$ leaves against measured
cubeful references.

**Primary metric.** Cube PR on the BGSage money benchmark, restricted to the 700
positions with rolled-out references — **n = 1,018 cube sub-decisions** — fed the
benchmark's own reference probabilities so the network's evaluation error is out
of the comparison. Baseline fixed before the run: $x = 0.68 \rightarrow$
**5.406 ± 0.609**. Variants are compared to it **paired**.

**Fit and confirm.** The fitted variants are fitted on a 50% split of *games* —
not positions, since several cube decisions can come from one game — and
confirmed on the held-out half. Selection happens on the confirm half.

**Fitting on the metric we report, deliberately.** Variants are fitted by
minimising cube PR, not equity RMSE. Only the no-double/double-take gap *near the
decision boundary* moves a decision, so an index that fits the equities better
can choose worse. PR is piecewise constant in the parameters, so the search is a
grid, and the multi-parameter variant uses coordinate descent — a coordinate-wise
minimum, not a certified global one.

**A coherence gate, applied before PR.** For one position,
$E_O \geq E_C \geq E_U$ must hold: owning the cube cannot be worth less than it
being centred, which cannot be worth less than the opponent owning it. Nothing in
the fitting enforces this, because each benchmark entry is *either* centred *or*
owned, so a variant fitted per cube state is fitted on disjoint position sets and
is free to come out incoherent — and PR cannot notice, since every decision it
scores involves one cube location at a time. **A variant that breaks the ordering
is disqualified regardless of its PR.**

**Variants.**

| variant | what it varies |
|---|---|
| `baseline` | $x = 0.68$ everywhere — GNUBG's published contact constant |
| `race_split` | $x = 0.60$ in race plans, 0.68 elsewhere — GNUBG's documented split |
| `refit_global` | one re-fitted index |
| `refit_per_state` | a re-fitted index per cube state |
| `dead` / `live` | $x = 0$ and $x = 1$ — the envelope the model interpolates between |
| `offset` | $x = 0.68$ plus a fitted additive shift to the no-double line |

**Conclusion template.** *"Is Janowski's cube-life index mis-set? → [answer]:
[variant] = [cube PR ± paired CI] against 5.406 for x = 0.68 (BGSage money
benchmark, measured references, n = 1,018 cube sub-decisions, fit and confirmed
on disjoint game splits)."*

## exp024 — results {#exp024-results}

**Yes, but re-fitting the index is a patch on the symptom.** A single re-fitted
index takes cube PR from 5.406 to 2.278, confirmed at **+3.206 ± 0.984** paired
on held-out games. The variant that scores *best* is disqualified for
incoherence, and that failure is the clearest evidence that $E_C$ — not the index
— is what is wrong.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
ORDER = ["baseline", "race_split", "offset", "refit_global", "refit_per_state",
         "live", "dead"]
NAMES = {"baseline": "x = 0.68 (published)",
         "race_split": "x = 0.60 race / 0.68 contact",
         "offset": "x = 0.68 + fitted offset",
         "refit_global": "refit one index",
         "refit_per_state": "refit index per cube state",
         "dead": "x = 0 (dead cube)",
         "live": "x = 1 (live cube)"}
print("| variant | fitted | cube PR | held-out PR | held-out paired | ordering |")
print("|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|")
for name in ORDER:
    r = variant("reference", name)
    a = r["variant"]
    if name == "refit_global":
        params = f"x = {a['x_nd_centered']:.3f}"
    elif name == "refit_per_state":
        params = (f"{a['x_nd_player']:.3f} / {a['x_nd_centered']:.3f} / "
                  f"{a['x_dt']:.3f}")
    elif name == "offset":
        params = f"{a['nd_offset']:+.3f}"
    else:
        params = "—"
    pd = r["confirm"]["paired_vs_baseline"]
    delta = "—" if name == "baseline" else f"{pd['delta_pr']:+.3f} ± {pd['delta_ci95']:.3f}"
    coh = r["coherence"]
    rate = f"{100 * coh['violation_rate']:.1f}%"
    flag = rate if coh["coherent"] else f"{rate} — **disqualified**"
    print(f"| {NAMES[name]} | {params} | {r['pr']:.3f} | {r['confirm']['pr']:.3f} | "
          f"{delta} | {flag} |")
```

**The best-scoring variant is not a cube model.** Fitting an index per cube state
scores 1.670 — the best number in the table — and puts the *centred* cube above
*owning* it on 90% of positions. It is three separate regressions on three
disjoint slices that were never required to agree, and PR could not see the
problem because no scored decision compares those two locations. It is rejected.

That failure is informative rather than merely embarrassing. A mis-set constant
does not produce an impossible ordering; a mis-specified form does. And the
mechanism is exactly what the three-formula measurement predicts: $x$ enters
$E_C$ and $E_O$ with the same sign, so pushing the centred index up to repair
$E_C$ lifts the centred curve straight through the one above it.

**A flat offset does not reproduce the gain either**, at +2.643 ± 1.396 against
+3.206 ± 0.984, so the residual is not a constant the index could have absorbed.
**GNUBG's race split does not help** on these decisions, the only variant failing
to beat the baseline.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Cube PR on held-out games, lower is better, with 95% intervals. Grey is the published constant and the variants that fail to beat it; blue is coherent and better; hatched is disqualified on the ordering constraint despite the best score. The dead- and live-cube references are omitted — at 11.2 and 8.3 they would flatten the rest."
show = ["baseline", "race_split", "offset", "refit_global", "refit_per_state"]
vals = [variant("reference", n)["confirm"]["pr"] for n in show]
errs = [variant("reference", n)["confirm"]["pr_ci95"] for n in show]
coh = [variant("reference", n)["coherence"]["coherent"] for n in show]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 2.8))
y = np.arange(len(show))
colours = [C_OWN if (c and n not in ("baseline", "race_split")) else "#9a9a9a"
           for n, c in zip(show, coh)]
bars = ax.barh(y, vals, xerr=errs, color=colours, height=0.62,
               error_kw={"ecolor": "#444444", "capsize": 3, "lw": 1})
for bar, c in zip(bars, coh):
    if not c:
        bar.set_hatch("///"); bar.set_edgecolor("#444444"); bar.set_facecolor("#d9d9d9")
ax.set_yticks(y, [NAMES[n] for n in show], fontsize=9)
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlabel("cube PR on held-out games (lower is better)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### Does it transfer off the reference probabilities?

Stage A held the probabilities fixed so only the cube model varied. The check is
to feed different probabilities through the same variant — Raccoon's own
six-outcome head, and GNUBG's at 0-ply — with the selected variant applied
unchanged, no per-engine re-fit.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
rows = [("GNUBG 0-ply", "gnubg-0ply", "baseline", "x = 0.68"),
        ("Raccoon ep22", "ep22", "baseline", "x = 0.68"),
        ("Raccoon ep22", "ep22", "selected", "x = 0.800 (selected)")]
print("| evaluations | cube model | cube PR (n = 1,018) |")
print("|---|---|---:|")
for label, src, name, model in rows:
    r = variant(src, name)
    print(f"| {label} | {model} | {r['pr']:.3f} ± {r['pr_ci95']:.3f} |")
sel = variant("ep22", "selected")["confirm"]["paired_vs_baseline"]
print(f"\nOn ep22's own evaluations the selected index is worth "
      f"**{sel['delta_pr']:+.3f} ± {sel['delta_ci95']:.3f}** on held-out games, "
      f"against +3.206 ± 0.984 on the reference probabilities it was fitted to — "
      f"the same gain on probabilities it never saw.")
```

> Is the index mis-set? → **Yes, and it is not the real problem.** One re-fitted
> index gives **2.278** cube PR against 5.406 at $x = 0.68$ (measured references,
> n = 1,018), **+3.206 ± 0.984** paired on held-out games. But the better-scoring
> per-state fit is incoherent on 90% of positions, and a flat offset falls short
> — both pointing at $E_C$'s form rather than its parameter.

## Where the model can improve

Re-fitting the constant is banked and it was cheap, but everything above says the
constant was never the real problem. Two of the three formulas are already right;
the work is on the third.

### Stop giving the dead branch a fixed share

Both measured defects trace to one choice, which makes them one target rather
than two. The model interpolates between a dead cube and a live cube with a
constant weight:

$$E = (1-x)\,E_{\text{dead}} + x\,E_{\text{live}}$$

A constant weight is defensible in the middle of the range, where whether you
extract the cube's value genuinely depends on getting future doubles right. It is
not defensible near the cash point, where the live branch has hit $+1$ and the
dead branch has not, and where the cube's value needs no future at all — you
double, your opponent passes, you have your point. The measured error has the shape
that mistake predicts: near zero where the two branches are close, sagging to
−0.083 for $E_O$ and −0.074 for $E_C$ where they are furthest apart.

The unresolved Jacoby question points the same way without settling it. The dead
branch zeroes gammons — correct for a cube that never turns, hard to defend at a
fixed 32% weight in a position about to be doubled — and simply un-zeroing them
does fit better, though not for the reason a clean Jacoby story would predict.
Both symptoms suggest the weight should track *how likely the cube is to stay
where it is*, which is a property of the position rather than a constant.

So the candidate is a weight that rises toward the live branch as the cube
becomes more certain to be turned, derived from the market-loss argument rather
than fitted. It has a free function where the current model has a free constant,
so it must be disciplined: **the two indices are pinned by measurement at
$x_1 = 0.715$ and $x_2 = 0.705$**, and any candidate either predicts the 42,636
observed equities or it does not. One falsifiable sub-prediction comes free: the
sag before the cash point should close. Whether it also resolves the gammon-
asymmetry residual is the test of whether that residual was ever a Jacoby effect.

Two further leads for the centred case specifically. Janowski derives $E_C$ by
interpolating four known points and says outright that no simple formula is
available — so the interpolation, not the concept, is the suspect. And the model
has **no Jacoby-valid centred form at all**, which is the case all money play
falls under.

**exp025**, and it is the one worth running first.

### Does whose turn it is matter?

A lead that fell out of using two datasets. The centred bias at the published
index is **+0.025** on post-move positions (opponent on roll) and **−0.072** on
pre-roll cube decisions. The sign flips.

Janowski's formulas take no account of whose turn it is; the probabilities are
supposed to carry it. If that is not sufficient — if a centred cube is
systematically worth more to the player on roll than the model allows — then part
of what looks like a broken $E_C$ is a missing term. This is a hypothesis from
two numbers on two different position distributions, so it is a lead and not a
finding, but it is cheap to test with the data already in hand.

### Measure volatility rather than proxying it

$x$ is supposed to encode volatility. The obvious cheap proxy is contact — how
entangled the two sides still are. It does not work:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
c = DIAG["correlations"]
print(f"The residual's correlation with contact is "
      f"**{c['residual_vs_contact']:+.3f}**. Best-fit index by contact "
      f"quintile:\n")
print("| contact | positions | best-fit x |")
print("|---|---:|---:|")
for q in DIAG["by_contact_quintile"]:
    print(f"| {q['contact_lo']:.2f}–{q['contact_hi']:.2f} | {q['n']:,} | "
          f"{q['best_x_by_rmse']:.3f} |")
```

No monotone trend and nothing worth exploiting. That is the argument for
measuring volatility directly — the standard deviation of the 0-ply value across
the 21 possible next rolls, about 21 batched evaluations per position, reusing
`raccoon/eval/luck.py` and `raccoon/search/expectimax.py`. **exp026**, after
exp025, because a better-measured $x$ still feeds whichever centred form we end
up with.

### Learn the correction

A small model could predict the residual from the six-outcome vector plus
position features rather than deriving it. The most powerful angle and the least
principled: it would fit BGSage's references including whatever is idiosyncratic
about them. **exp027**, and only if the derivations fail.

## What search does instead — and why it is not the answer here

GNUBG and XG deal with $E_C$'s weakness by not relying on it. They run a cubeful
search and apply Janowski only at the leaves, so the formula's error is diluted by
lookahead rather than fixed. That is the same shape of answer
[exp021](search.qmd) found for checker play.

It is worth being clear that this is a *diagnosis*, not the goal. Adding search
routes around the closed form; it does not improve it. And the closed form is
what everything without a deep search depends on — fast analysis, the leaves of
the search itself, and every position where a cube decision must be made in the
time a human waits. Making the map better is the more useful result, and a search
inherits the improvement rather than removing the need for it.

## A separate cost: cube-blind checker play

One cost sits outside all of the above, because no cube model touches it. An
engine that ranks candidate *moves* by cubeless equity plays the checkers wrong
whatever its cube model does: the best move with the cube in the middle is not
always the best move when your opponent owns a 4-cube, because one line cashes
safely and the other plays for a gammon you can no longer collect.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(f"A perfect *cubeless* checker player scores **PR {FLOOR['pr']:.3f} "
      f"± {FLOOR['pr_ci95']:.3f}** on the cubeful metric "
      f"(n={FLOOR['n']:,} decisions). The cubeless-best and cubeful-best moves "
      f"differ on **{FLOOR['decisions_where_best_move_differs']:,} "
      f"({100 * FLOOR['fraction_differs']:.1f}%)** of them.\n")
print("| where the cube is | decisions | PR thrown away |")
print("|---|---:|---:|")
for owner in ("centered", "player", "opponent"):
    v = FLOOR["by_cube_owner"][owner]
    print(f"| {owner} | {v['n']:,} | {v['pr']:.3f} |")
```

Concentrated exactly where intuition says: with the cube centred there is
everything to play for, and in a pure race (0.046) it nearly vanishes. Ranking
moves by cubeful equity is a small change to `raccoon/train/lookahead.py` with a
bounded, already quantified prize — **exp028**. It is engine work rather than
model work, which is why it is noted here and not pursued above.

This also settles a comparison that has been quietly wrong. Raccoon's headline PR
of 0.95 is scored against *cubeless* references, while BGSage and XG quote PR
against cubeful ones and include cube decisions in the average. Those are
different metrics on different decision sets and should never have been read side
by side.

## What this page does not establish

* The references are **rollouts under Janowski-quality cube play**, not optimal
  cube play. The bots deciding when to double inside each rollout use the model
  being tested. This understates what a better model could reach rather than
  overstating it, but it is not distance-to-truth.
* Every measured position is a **post-move** position for the equity fit and a
  pre-roll one for the cube-PR test. The two are related but not identical, and
  the sign flip noted above is a live warning about mixing them.
* **No position is observed at two cube locations**, so the ordering constraint
  is a model check and can never be validated against data.
* The benchmark's cube positions are **selected for being non-trivial**, so
  indices fitted on them are tuned for close decisions and should not be quoted
  as general-purpose constants.
* Coordinate descent on a grid finds a **coordinate-wise minimum**, not a
  certified global one.
* Everything is **cubeless money play with Jacoby and beavers on**. Match play
  changes every take point and is untouched here.

## References

* Rick Janowski, *Take-Points in Money Games*
  ([PDF](https://bkgm.com/articles/Janowski/cubeformulae.pdf)) — the cube-life
  index, equations (5)–(7) for the three cube locations, the refined model of
  Appendix 2, and the Jacoby factors of Appendix 3.
* Keeler and Spencer, *Optimal Doubling in Backgammon* (1975)
  ([online](https://bkgm.com/articles/KeelerSpencer/OptimalDoublingInBackgammon/index.html))
  — the continuous model behind the live-cube take point.
* Lasse Hjorth Madsen, *Janowski Formulas*
  ([bganalyses](https://lassehjorthmadsen.github.io/bganalyses/)) — a worked
  comparison of what XG and GNU Backgammon report against the formulas, including
  the match-play extension this page does not attempt.
* [GNU Backgammon manual](https://www.gnu.org/software/gnubg/manual/gnubg.html)
  — the published 0.68 contact and 0.60 race indices.
